questions.q: On Instance A (the 4-cycle graph), what was QAOA p=1's expected cost at the depth-1-optimal angles, versus its best-of-10-shots result?
options: Expected cost ≈2.9996 (ratio 0.75), but best-of-10-shots found the true optimum of 4
Expected cost ≈4.0, identical to the best-of-shots result
Expected cost ≈2.0, and best-of-shots never found better than 2
Expected cost and best-of-shots were both exactly 3.0
questions.explain: The expected cost averaged over the full measurement distribution was ≈2.9996, but because the two optimal bitstrings together carried about 53% of the probability, sampling just 10 simulated shots already found the true optimum of 4.

questions.q: Why does the lab report two different QAOA numbers (expected cost and best-of-shots) rather than just one?
options: Because reporting only the expected cost would understate QAOA's practical usefulness, while reporting only best-of-shots would overstate how reliably a single shot lands on the optimum -- both numbers tell a different, necessary part of the story
Because the two numbers are actually identical and reporting both is redundant
Because QAOA cannot produce an expected cost value under any circumstances
Because best-of-shots is always a less meaningful metric than expected cost in every context
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls out that showing only one of these two numbers would bias the picture in one direction or the other -- exactly the kind of metric-selection fairness issue Lesson 21 warns about.

questions.q: On Instance B (the 5-node graph), which method or methods matched the true optimum of 5 reliably, and which did not?
options: Simulated annealing reliably reached 5 across multiple seeds; greedy from a worst-case start got stuck at 4
Greedy reliably reached 5 from every starting point; simulated annealing failed every time
Neither greedy nor simulated annealing ever reached the true optimum of 5
Both greedy and simulated annealing always matched the true optimum of 5 on every start
questions.explain: As established in Lesson 20, simulated annealing reliably reached the true optimum of 5 from the same point where greedy got stuck at 4 -- this lab's table reflects that same, previously-verified result.

questions.q: Why would presenting this lab's table as simply 'QAOA beats greedy and matches SA' be an incomplete or misleading summary, even if every individual number is accurate?
options: Because the lab deliberately never ran SA on Instance A or QAOA on Instance B, so no head-to-head comparison between QAOA and SA on the same instance actually exists in this data, and the problem sizes tested are far too small to generalize from
Because every number in the table is actually incorrect
Because greedy was never run in this lab at all
Because QAOA's best-of-shots result was not actually the true optimum
questions.explain: The table reports QAOA's result only on Instance A and SA's result only on Instance B -- there is no instance where both were directly compared -- and both instances are tiny, so neither Lesson 21's 'same instance' requirement nor its 'representative scale' requirement is satisfied by this summary.

questions.q: What limitation does the lab flag regarding the QAOA numbers and the classical angle-optimization step from Lesson 8?
options: The lab's QAOA numbers assume good angles (gamma, beta) are already known, and don't include the classical optimization cost that would be needed to find those angles on a new, unseen problem
QAOA requires no classical optimization step at all in this lab or in general
The classical angle-optimization step was fully timed and included in the comparison table
Angle optimization is only relevant for VQE, never for QAOA
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly notes that this comparison assumes the optimal angles are already known, omitting the real cost of finding them via classical optimization (Lesson 8) on a genuinely new problem -- a real limitation of this specific benchmark, not a hidden strength being claimed.
